topic: making straw bee skeps: coiling to a girth, bramble binding, hiving swarms and judging stores by weight

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: waga sprezynowa przy drzwiach szopy (waga ula zajeta w en-03)

base: I have begun making straw skeps for my swarms and the coils will not lie flat as they rise.
A bait hive sits in the old orchard and has taken a swarm for me two summers running.
A spring balance hangs by the shed door so that I can weigh each skep as it fills.
My first skep is broad at the base but narrows too quickly once I am four coils up.
Is that the fault of my girth, or am I drawing the straw too tightly at the turn?
It is the girth, almost certainly, since that ring alone decides the thickness of every coil you lay.
Pull each handful through the same girth and the coils will keep an even thickness the whole way up.
Narrowing comes from taking less straw as the hand tires, which happens to everybody at first.
Judge the coil by the ring and never by eye, because the eye grows generous as you go.
I made a proper girth out of a cow horn and the coils now come out very even.
The spring balance shows the finished skep at barely three pounds, which seems light to me.
The binding of split bramble keeps splitting itself whenever I draw it through the coil below.
Should the bramble be soaked first, or am I splitting it too thin to take the strain?
Soak the bramble overnight and split it into three, not into two as most people begin.
Thin bramble is stronger than thick, because the pith in a heavy strip breaks under the pull.
Draw it through with a bone bodkin and keep the shiny side outward as you bind.
A skep bound with dry bramble will loosen within a month and let the coils slide apart.
Soaking the bramble made all the difference and the binding no longer splits on me.
The first skep has stood a full season and the coils have not moved at all.
The bait hive took another swarm in June, which I hived into my second skep.
The bees have built comb hard against the walls and I cannot lift the skep to look.
How am I to judge the stores without cutting into the comb along the side?
Weight is the whole of it, and a hefted skep tells you more than any look inside.
A good skep of bees in autumn should feel like a full bucket of water when lifted.
Weigh it, note the figure and weigh again in a month, since the fall matters more than the number.
If the weight drops away fast in October you have a colony that will not see the spring.
Feed then, and not in January, because syrup taken late is never properly stored away.
I weighed the skep in September and again a month later and it had lost two pounds.
That seemed a fair fall, so I fed thick syrup until the weight had come back up.
The colony came through the winter and threw a strong swarm at the end of May.
Should I let that swarm build its own comb, or give it a start from the old skep?
Let it build its own, since a swarm draws comb faster than at any other time of its life.
Comb cut from an old skep sags and carries whatever the last colony left behind in it.
Set the new skep on a clean board and shade it for the first week or so.
Fresh comb built in June will carry that colony for the next four or five years.
The swarm drew its comb in a fortnight and filled the skep almost down to the board.
I now have three skeps and would like to take honey without destroying any colony.
My grandfather used to drive the bees upward into an empty skep set above the full one.
Is driving still worth doing, or is it more trouble than the honey is worth?
Driving is worth it, and with straw it is the only decent way to take a crop.
Set the empty skep mouth to mouth above the full one and drum steadily on the sides.
The bees walk up within ten minutes, and you take the lower skep with no loss at all.
Do it on a warm afternoon in August, so the driven colony still has time to build.
